goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.

gold_reference: A strong answer argues that even a tiny SaaS team can sell to a CIO, but only when the founder understands the buyer's social contract: do not create career risk, be honest about what is missing, show fast ROI, and build trust directly. answer:
Can a startup really sell to the CIO? I know many founders think so. And if they do get on a plane and fly out to meet a potential big deal … well, most likely they’ll just blow it. Because what’s a “big deal” to a CEO isn’t necessarily what matters to IT. In fact, sales cycles can often seem like almost nothing to some CEOs (I remember when we were acquired by Adobe, our CEO thought there was no way the acquisition could happen because the legal team took too much time), while others have been burned by startups before. So who knows? It’s tough. But here’s my rule for selling to a CIO:
It depends on how small you are
. Here’s why. When a tech startup approaches a Big Tech Company for a partnership, the first thing they want to know is How Many People Will This Take Up in Our Organization? Or What Budget Will This Take? That makes sense from their side. They have limited bandwidth and budget. So they ask about headcount. They ask about dollars. Now let’s say you’re Salesforce, and the start-up wants to integrate into your platform. Let’s say you have hundreds of engineers already working full-time on integrations and APIs. Well, they might tell you something like “Hey, we don’t need anything for now, thanks”. Or they might tell you that yes, they’d love to work together, but they need access to another department. Or whatever. Point is, they will push back, and hard, until they figure out where it fits on their org chart. But now imagine you’re an 8-person startup, maybe even smaller.

So there’s a strategy exercise I like to go through with startups I’ve invested in that are past $20m-$30m ARR or so:
Who would you buy with 10% of your market cap?
I.e., who would you give 10% of your company away to buy?  It turns out this is an important threshold.  The SEC generally defines this as “material”.  It’s also enough of your company that everyone will suffer a lot of dilution, and enough that you can’t do more than a handful of these deals ever.  Versus later, when you are bigger, you can do a ton of tiny acquisitions.  If you are worth $10 Billion and buy a small startup for, say $50m, really, you’ll never notice the dilution or, in some cases, even the cash spent.
But I like this exercise because it focuses founders that are starting to achieve scale on maybe just one out-of-the-box idea for combining with someone to do something even bigger and better.
And now is a good time to think about this.  Times are tougher, and egos are muted.  Now might be a good time to buy one of your top partners, a smaller but scrappier competition, or someone that’s built that key part of your vision that you yourself haven’t been able to build.

Some have become close friends who keep me honest on everything from product strategy to hiring decisions. But here’s what many people get wrong about selling enterprise software: It’s rarely about winning deals through pure technology superiority or innovative features. It’s often about understanding the social contract. What do I mean by “social contract”? In complex B2B buying processes (think Fortune 50 enterprises), there’s almost always someone else involved besides the actual end-user. This could be a procurement team member, an IT manager, a business stakeholder, or even multiple stakeholders across different departments. Each of these individuals brings their own motivations, constraints, and priorities to the table. And when they’re making recommendations to their boss—the CIO—they need reasons beyond just saying “this looks cool.” They need stories they can tell that help justify why something should make it into the budget. Here’s how it works in practice: When a CIO walks into the room where the final decision will be made, they don’t just want to hear about innovation. They want to see how the solution fits into their broader goals—and if it does, they’ll find ways to backfill the gaps. I was at Dreamforce a few years ago when I had my first interaction with a CIO. It was a big deal for me because up until then I'd never met a CIO. Never really heard what they thought, how they think, and what their problems were. And this particular CIO just kind of blew me away by saying something like "I used to buy Salesforce licenses myself, now we have such a large enterprise agreement that nobody knows where all those seats actually go."
And he said, "We're going through budget cuts right now, so we need to reduce our headcount." He looked around the room and said, "That means some people here will lose their jobs today."
He walked out of the meeting room and the rest of us sat there in stunned silence. We didn't know quite what to do next. But that moment was formative for me. It taught me that software executives work under different social contracts than consumer companies and even most SaaS companies. Their job security comes from delivering on-time features, building reliable systems, reducing operational complexity, and demonstrating clear value over time. Not from shipping great products quickly, growing fast, or achieving perfect unit economics.
The CIO's Job Is Getting Harder
Let me tell you why CIOs matter more than ever:
They've been doing layoffs every quarter since '22
Their budgets have shrunk significantly in real terms
CFOs have taken control of IT spending decisions across the board
There are fewer and fewer new tech vendors being allowed into organizations
It's harder to get meetings with CIOs
Mostly they don't want to meet with start-ups anymore
Many top CIOs have moved to a "cut-cut" mode - cutting everything

Who would you buy with 10% of your market cap?

answer:
So we’ve done so many SaaStr deep dives with Monday’s founders and CEO Eran Zinman here:
#1.  Even today, 85% of their new customers have never used a project management tool before
. That’s how simple Monday makes it. And yet … they can still drive up ACVs over time. A reminder no matter what category you’re in, if you solve a real problem for real folks — there will always be room to grow ACVs even after initial adoption.
#2.  80% of all sales reps close 100%
This isn’t unusual per se, but I love seeing it called out again and again across so many different B2B leaders. It shows how important training, onboarding, etc. are. If 80% of your reps are closing, then the ones that don’t need some help. Some investment.
#3.  25% of customers now start off using Free
Monday didn’t do much marketing until later (more on that below), so free was key to getting folks into the system. They often stayed paid, however, once they added multiple users.
#4.  60% of customers use more than one Monday product
. This is pretty common, but I loved seeing this tracked over time. Many SaaS companies don’t track usage across products as well as they should IMHO, because they want each team to manage its own product. But if you sell to larger customers, you should. At least track cross-product usage at a high level, and incent teams to work together here. You’ll learn where the big synergies are, especially if you are selling to bigger customers.
#5.  “Growth Matters More Than Almost Anything Else”
. Ahem. We like to say the same thing, Eran! 😉
And a few other interesting notes:

#6.  Monday.com was profitable for years before IPO’ing
. Another good lesson that while going public is very helpful, it doesn’t change everything. In fact, profitability usually means higher multiples when you go public.

answer:
So we've talked quite a bit over time with many leaders in SaaS about how they're doing things right now. And I wanted to dig into our latest episode, which was with Monday dot com co-founder and CEO Eran Zinman. It's a great conversation because Eran came back after being out for several years, joined his old company when it was at like five million dollars in ARR, and took it all the way to over $500 million today.
And he just shared so much good stuff. Let me pull out some top learnings. Number one, it turns out growth still matters. I know there's a lot of different opinions in the markets right now, but boy, it sure seems like if you want to go big, you need to keep growing fast. Because even though Monday had incredible retention of 120%, it wasn't enough. It was only 25%. So if they'd grown 60%, they would have doubled their business, right? But they didn't grow 60%—they grew 90%. Now they're worth 30 billion dollars. That's kind of interesting math.
Number two, the bigger deals matter most in SaaS. We learned this with Zoom, we learned this with Slack, we learned it with Salesforce. You really need to focus on going bigger and bigger in SaaS. And Mondays has followed that playbook. They went from selling mostly to SMBs early on to focusing more and more on larger companies. Today, 75% of their revenue comes from customers spending more than $50,00 a year. This is important. This is why you need to go upmarket earlier than ever before. Otherwise, everyone gets left behind.
Number three, marketing can be incredibly efficient. Yes, it costs money to get leads and customers. But it doesn't always cost that much. In fact, in some cases, it costs less than nothing. How does that work? Well, you don't invest in marketing if you're already profitable.

answer:
How to Truly Stand Out in Any Job Interview, From SDR to CMO
We’ve all been there. You’re prepping for a critical interview – whether it’s for a first-time entry-level gig or a stretch position that’ll catapult your career – and you’re stuck wondering what makes you truly special.
The truth? Most candidates fall into the same traps:
Generic answers to behavioral questions
Lack of genuine passion about the company and role
Inadequate preparation that leaves them scrambling during the conversation
But here’s what separates the winners from the also-rans:
they show up prepared to genuinely help solve real problems. Let me break down exactly how to nail this approach, using my recent experience interviewing SDRs as a perfect case study.
Your #1 Job Before Any Interview: Help Solve Problems They Are Having
Before I even sat down for any candidate interviews recently, they’d already done their homework.  Almost every single one had read our website, watched some videos, joined LinkedIn, etc.  And then … they’d sent us ideas on how we could do better!
Here were some great ones:
“Hey Jason,
I noticed you have no presence on TikTok. As someone who works with Gen Z talent, I think you should consider having a strong online presence across multiple platforms.”
Or:
“I was browsing through your blog posts and saw you mentioned something about needing to improve SEO. Have you considered focusing more on long-form content versus short social media posts?”
These weren’t generic “tell me why you’d be a good fit” responses. These were specific observations followed by actionable suggestions.
And guess what? In almost every case, the candidate got invited back for another round because they showed they cared enough to actually understand the business challenges beyond just filling a role.

Dear SaaStr: What’s the Best Way to Help Top SDRs Become SMB Account Execs?
The best way to prepare a top-performing SDR for an SMB AE role is to give them a structured path that builds on their strengths while exposing them to the full sales cycle.
And
most
of the best will want a promotion path.  Most.
Here’s how I’d approach it:
1. Let Them Ride Shotgun on Deals
:
Pair them with an experienced AE and let them shadow the entire sales process—from discovery calls to closing. This “ride shotgun” approach gives them a front-row seat to learn how deals are negotiated, objections are handled, and relationships are built. It’s critical they see how to take a lead from qualification to close.
2. Gradual Ownership of Deals:
Start by letting them handle smaller, simpler deals or specific parts of the sales process, like running demos or managing follow-ups. This builds confidence and gives them hands-on experience without overwhelming them.
3. Mentorship and Coaching:
Assign them a mentor—ideally a high-performing SMB AE—who can provide guidance, feedback, and support. Regular one-on-ones to review progress and address challenges are key.
4. Sales Training:
Invest in formal sales training focused on SMB sales. This should include objection handling, negotiation tactics, and closing strategies. The goal is to bridge the gap between their BDR skills (prospecting, qualifying) and the skills needed to close deals.

answer:
So we've all been there.
We're going into a big interview. And then, right after we meet, our competitor gets hired over us. We don't understand why. And sometimes even worse, when we get passed over for something, it happens again.
And again. For years and years. Even decades.
What did I do wrong? What should I have done differently?
I remember my first big management meeting when I was promoted to be Director of Product. I had never managed anyone before. Never really. So they brought me a very smart guy who used to work at Google.
He'd just left his last company where he'd built some amazing things.
And within six months, he'd basically built all this stuff himself. He didn't need any help anymore. But he wasn't happy enough. He wanted more.
It made sense. He deserved it.
But what I learned later, looking back, was that this manager — he never got told anything good. No matter how great the quarter was, no matter how many features were shipped, no matter how much customers loved him. They always found fault.
In his bosses. In engineering. Everyone else.
That became sort of my mini-mantra. Be positive. Because otherwise, folks won't see the great stuff.
The world needs a bit less criticism and negativity.
Fast forward to today, we now know so much more than ever. And yet so much still isn't working in hiring. Too often, we just aren't using the tools available to us.
Let me share five learnings:

The Wild Ride of Informatica: 32 Years, 2 IPOs, to $8 Billion Acquisition by Salesforce
In the pantheon of enterprise software companies, few have experienced the rollercoaster ride that is Informatica. Founded in 1988 by Gaurav Dhillon and Diaz Nesamoney (who was just 19 when they started), Informatica began life as a data warehousing company during the golden age of CRM. What followed would span three decades, two IPOs, multiple transformations, and finally, an $8 billion acquisition by Salesforce – marking perhaps the most dramatic exit in B2B history. But here’s what makes Informatica truly remarkable: this isn’t just another tech story. It’s a masterclass in how to build sustainable value over time through relentless execution, strategic positioning, and smart timing. Let’s take a deep dive into the fascinating journey of how two college roommates built something that would become an essential infrastructure layer for modern enterprise applications. Early Days and First IPO (1990-2001)
Founded in February 1990 by Gaurav Dhillon and his roommate, Diaanese Nesamoney (then just 19), who met on their first day at Stanford University, Informatica emerged from the classic Silicon Valley playbook. These young entrepreneurs identified a painful problem: data management was becoming increasingly complex as organizations moved beyond simple transactional systems toward business intelligence capabilities. Their initial product, PowerCenter, wasn’t revolutionary—it was evolutionary. As David Sacks noted, “Data replication is kind of boring stuff,” yet it represented exactly the sort of foundational technology that large enterprises needed.

The key insight
:
There’s a difference between companies that “matter” (platform-shifting, $100+ billion market cap potential) and companies that are “perfectly good businesses” ($5-15 billion market cap, consistent returns).
Both can make investors and founders wealthy, but the strategies for optimizing each are different.
What Actually Matters: The Uncomfortable Truth About Impact
The conversation took a philosophical turn when discussing what companies actually “matter” in the grand scheme of technological progress.  Sam Lessin argues with Jason and the group about how meaninful SaaS is.
The harsh reality
:
Most companies, even successful ones, don’t fundamentally change the world. Lessin argued Box, despite being a well-run public company worth $5+ billion, probably doesn’t “matter” in the sense of being paradigm-shifting.
But here’s the nuance
:
Not mattering in a historical sense doesn’t mean not being valuable. As one investor put it: “If the $14 billion market cap was in my bank account, I would think it was a very important company indeed.”
For SaaS founders, this creates two strategic paths:
Build for infinity
:
Go after platform-shifting opportunities where you could fundamentally change how an industry works (think Salesforce in the early 2000s)
Build for excellence
:
Create a phenomenal business in a defined market, optimize for profitability and exits, and don’t apologize for being “just” a great business
The mistake
:
Trying to split the difference. Either embrace the infinity bet with appropriate risk tolerance and capital requirements, or build a capital-efficient business optimized for strong returns.

.

.

.

and I thought what would be great was to do a deep dive into some of the most popular videos over time, because they're always changing.
The ones that used to be super popular aren't quite so much anymore, although there still are some all-time favorites out there.
And then new things have risen to the top.
I think you'll find them very interesting, especially if you haven't watched many SaaStr sessions yet, like me.
They've been really good.
We had some classic sessions early on, and maybe a few of those will interest you even today.
But also, I think the newer sessions and topics might help you see how far we've grown and matured as content creators.
There were three sessions way back when that were super popular.
Our first session ever was with Adyam.
It was a really fun one.
Harry came down to San Francisco, and we did a deep dive together.
What I remember about it, which I didn't know before doing this exercise, is how different my slides look now versus back then.
This is sort of early days.
My slides looked totally different than they do now.
That was probably helpful.
Then another one that was pretty cool and something we talked about again recently was how to build a business that scales with your customers.
Zendesk's CTO came down and spoke at SaaStr.
Those are two sessions that you can go back and watch that have stood the test of time.
One thing that's changed since then, though, is that the talks are more polished.
Everyone's gotten better at editing and making their presentations easier to listen to.
Another thing that's changed is that the speakers don't use as much humor.
Humor can make a presentation more enjoyable to listen to.
The older videos sometimes feel a bit slower paced.
Things move faster now.
Some of our best sessions over the years have included folks that have gone through hyper growth, including Klaviyo, who went from zero to almost $200 million in revenue.
I mean, that's insane.
I'm sure they wouldn't say it themselves, but it's crazy.
Totango also went through rapid growth and joined us later.
FlyWheel, Monday dot com, and others have done incredible jobs scaling up and growing rapidly.
These were some of the top sessions, but here's the thing:
newer sessions continue to rise to the top.
One that's relatively recent is the top five mistakes that Monday made during scale.
This is one of my favorite sessions, actually.
There's a lot that resonates with me, especially being part of a big company.
It's tough, but it makes sense.
Also, one of the more recent sessions on early gains, early pains is also a great one.
I'd recommend watching that if you're going through hyper growth right now.

answer:
So I’ve been doing SaaS since 2005, investing since 2010, building startups since then too (and before). And we’re coming up on $30B in ARR across B2B software! And what do I see? The biggest change in how founders sell to customers … ever:
Customers buying much faster than they used to. Yes, yes, there’s still a lot of inertia out there. But in many categories, especially with AI-enhanced apps — customers are buying far faster today than even 12 months ago. We were all waiting so long for budget cycles, and to get into procurement processes, etc. It’s just taking longer now to close deals than it was 18-24 months ago. Customers don’t care anymore if the product isn’t perfect when they start deploying. They will build around rough products that aren’t truly ready yet. This doesn’t mean customers don’t want great solutions. They do. But they’ll deploy something today that does most of what they need, rather than waiting until later when it might be better. Customers expect a demo to be pretty slick already
. So much has changed in GTM over the past few years, but demos haven’t. That’s why demos seem like they have gotten worse. Before, prospects would often wait weeks to try out your product. Today, they demand a demo in minutes. That means the app itself needs to be pretty polished, at least enough to make sense. Otherwise, folks won’t take time. Customers expect things to just work well today. In my first startup job, back in ’05, our product didn’t really work very well. But because deployment was manual, it took us days to set up anything new. Fast forward to today, AI has made deployment instant, so customers expect it to Just Work. So if it doesn’t, they move on.

answer: Why Now Is The Biggest Change in SaaS Sales in 15+ Years We’ve never seen anything like today in B2B software sales since I started investing back around 2008-2009 or so. At first, the change was subtle. It started with customers asking to talk to someone else on our team. Then they asked if we had anyone better. And then they just wanted to buy direct from us - without ever talking to sales. That’s when things changed from being mostly transactional to relational selling. But that wasn’t really until the past few years. Today, it seems almost everyone wants to skip sales altogether now. They want to go straight to a free trial or pilot. Or even go around us entirely and try to buy from an agent or AI. What happened? Well, two main factors. First, sales reps stopped caring. Many stopped caring because there weren’t enough leads anymore. When there were tons of leads in the Boom Times of 2018-2020, every rep could close 10 deals a month easily. So many “bad” reps stayed. Those that didn’t care. Then when lead flow slowed down after Covid hit, most couldn’t figure out how to sell. Many stopped caring. You have to care to win in sales. Second, buyers got smarter. Buyers became much savvier over the past 5+ years. Many went from having 100s of potential vendors they could use (in vertical SaaS) to 50-100 options, and finally, down to fewer than 10. Even fewer for bigger deals.

answer: So I've been investing in startups since '97 and have never seen anything quite like what we're seeing today. It's the biggest change in SaaS sales in maybe ever. And I'm not just talking about AI here, although that's part of it. But I'm really talking about how much easier it is to buy software now than even two years ago, and probably three years ago. Not every category, obviously, but many categories. Let me just show you some examples. First, let me tell you where things were in the old days, when I first started doing B2B SaaS way back when. Way back then, if you wanted to sell something to someone, you'd go out there and get them on Zoom. They wouldn't want to take a call, they'd say "No, I'll do email." You'd send them an email. Email was terrible because you had to keep following up with them multiple times. That would create anxiety. It created anxiety for the buyer too because they knew they weren't going to respond right away. The emails pile up. It creates anxiety for everyone involved. Then they might finally agree to meet you in person. Oh great, thank goodness! You schedule a meeting and hope they show up. If they don't show up, well, tough luck. But when they did show up, you'd try to do demos live. You could demo it yourself pretty quickly, especially if you didn't have a big team behind you. Or sometimes you'd bring in a third party to help you, which sort of helps, but you still got to learn the product cold. So the average deal closed over Zoom used to take weeks. Maybe months. Sometimes longer. And after all those steps, after all the pain, once the buyer decided they wanted to use your app, they'd pay upfront. Every month. Usually annually. Maybe quarterly.

answer:
So there’s been a lot of worry among VCs lately around public multiples — how much value a VC pays today might look silly if the startup were able to IPO down the road.
Look, I get it.  Yes, Palantir trades at $250 Billion today.  But … that doesn’t mean everything is worth $200B+ ARR times 10x.
But …
I’ve talked to so many founders that aren’t worried.  At all.  Why?  Because they don’t see what their investors do here:
They don’t think they’ll ever IPO.  They just plain don’t care.  And they also don’t believe their current valuations will hold up even if they did IPO.  So again, why should they worry?  This isn’t them.  Not really.
Should you worry about the impact of public market multiples on your valuation?  Probably not too much.  Unless you can truly imagine going public someday yourself.
What you probably need to worry about way more is that your burn rate keeps accelerating past 18-24 months
— because then you won’t have enough cash left.  The burn rate is still high across SaaS overall, and many Cloud leaders like Datadog, Snowflake, etc. continue to grow faster than anyone expected pre-Covid.  And yet … they’re burning tons of money along the way.   A record amount actually.
At some point, most startups simply run out of cash.  That stressor is real, and it happens every year.
And finally, should you worry when your VCs start leaving?  Maybe yes.  But only after they leave.  It almost never helps.

These are Strange Times Indeed in SaaS and Cloud.  SaaS is back, and AI is hot.  But times are still challenging for many.  And competition is fiercer than ever.
If things are in any way challenging, and you might need to raise more money — perhaps most important of all is keeping your existing investors’ confidence.
Your existing investors are the ones that often will bring you the leads for the next financing round.  And most importantly, any new investors and leaders will reach out to them for diligence checks on how the company is doing.  You want them to be SuperFans.  Even, and perhaps especially, when times are a bit bumpy.
Your investors are wired to understand you may not hit the plan for the year
Where they lose confidence is if:
– You sort of hide it
– You are running out of money
Run toward Bad News.  Not from it.

And most VCs are used to tougher times, and a missed quarter, and a botched hire or two.  That isn’t what undermines confidence.  Lack of vision, honesty, and transparency do.
So here’s a quick checklist of what undermines confidence in your existing investors:

1. Surprises
. Every VC expects a rough quarter or two, and even a rough year.  But as founders, you should know well ahead of time.  Nothing undermines confidence more than an out-of-the-blue email that growth plummeted. This spooks investors most of all. Give everyone multiple heads-ups early.

2. Lack of a (realistic) plan
.  What’s your realistic plan to grow faster?

So we’ve taken a look at many SaaS leaders over the years on their way to $1B+ ARR … but few have gotten less attention than Atlassian.
It’s been quietly building itself into a global powerhouse.  It IPO’d back in 2015 and crossed $1B ARR around then.  Fast forward to today, it’s approaching almost $3 Billion in ARR, growing a stunning 32%, and worth a cool $110 Billion (!).
And yet … it still isn’t quite getting the same level of attention as say, HubSpot, Monday.com, etc.
Let’s take a closer look!
Atlassian was founded way back in 2002 by two engineers who were frustrated with software development tools. They created Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Trello, and several other products designed specifically for software teams. Their mission has remained consistent: “to help every team unleash its full potential.”
Here Are 5 Key Takeaways:
#1. Product Diversification Has Been a Masterstroke – But Not Without Its Headwinds
The Numbers Don’t Lie:
Jira Cloud
has grown substantially, increasing its contribution to Atlassian’s revenue mix
Trello Business Class
continues to grow rapidly
Stash
is gaining traction (even though it hasn’t had much impact)
Bitbucket
remains strong
Confluence
had modest growth despite the challenges
But here’s what’s interesting—while product diversification has clearly paid off, it hasn’t solved all problems. One major challenge? Getting developers to adopt new workflows. Developers can be notoriously resistant to change! As one industry observer noted, “Developers are known to resist new technologies, so adoption will likely continue to be challenging.”

So there was just so much great stuff coming out of SaaStr Annual recently, we wanted to take some time to go through our top learnings from Atlassian. And they're pretty interesting because Atlassian's grown into what will soon be a $3 billion run rate company, maybe even earlier than that, all while being incredibly profitable. So let's dig in.
Number one: 100% of their growth comes from $10k+ customers. That's right, if you sell SMBs, forget it, it's too late for you. It doesn't matter how many free editions, it doesn't matter how many freemium deals, it doesn't matter how many tiny little customers you get. No, no, no. Because if you don't have a strong enough product, if you can't close larger logos, then eventually you're dead. Because those folks won't buy from you anymore.
Second, seat expansion drives growth. I know a lot of founders resist this, especially when you have low ACVs like Atlassian does. They say, "I want to charge per seat." Well, look, you got to do that sometimes. But Atlassian proves that it works. And the key here is it's not the individual seats themselves that drive growth. It's the fact that over time, you need more seats across your entire customer base.
Third, 47% of their revenue comes from outside North America. Now I think most of us are still very U.S.-centric. We're used to getting a lot of funding from Silicon Valley, San Francisco Bay Area companies, people who speak English natively. But 47%? Wow! You gotta build global products early, my friends.
Fourth, $1 million plus customers are their fastest growing segment. Look, this is where things change.

answer:
Q:  I’m At Risk Of Being an NRR Zombie — Should I Just Give Up?
An NRR zombie isn’t just losing customers. They aren’t even really leaving. It’s worse. The churn is masked by upsells. But still, over time, the base contracts down, because the core product becomes less valuable to the customer. And they don’t renew their smaller deals. So if you have < 100% NRR overall … that means each year, you lose all those customers who didn’t expand …
and another big chunk of your existing base due to not renewing. That can compound to some pretty scary losses, especially once your initial momentum runs out. Your job is to get those renewal customers back, too. To keep them. Not just the ones you manage to upsell to more seats today. The good news? Most folks stop trying after they’ve lost a few years of net negative churn. After all, when your NRR drops below 110%, it gets harder and harder every year to make up for those losses. Once your NRR falls below 100% overall, each year your base shrinks. Each year, it gets harder to hit next year’s plan. Here’s what I’d suggest:
First,
you need to invest much more aggressively here than you probably want to. You need to hire someone great here
. Someone with experience in driving NRR and Renewals up. Ideally, someone with experience doing better than you are now. Second,
your VP Customer Success needs to take responsibility here
. This is her/his job. Not to drive NPS (although important). But to increase NRR / Net Revenue Retention. Third,
you need to set aside budget to help retain the smaller accounts
. These guys will leave without help. And they’ll leave quietly. You won’t know until later. Fourth,
invest heavily in account expansion
.

answer: What to Do If You’re An NRR Zombie It’s time to take action if your net retention rate (NRR) isn’t growing despite investing heavily in product development and marketing. Here’s how to address it effectively: First, acknowledge that you can't outspend your way back to healthy NRR. The days of just hiring more people to boost NRR are behind us. Instead, focus on retaining existing customers by improving their experience with your product. Second, understand why NRR is declining. Is it due to increased competition, poor product quality, lack of innovation, high churn, low upsells, or something else? Once you identify the root cause, develop a comprehensive plan to address it. Third, invest in customer success and support to ensure your customers feel valued and heard. This includes providing timely assistance, regular check-ins, and proactive outreach to prevent dissatisfaction. Fourth, review your pricing strategy to ensure it remains competitive while maintaining profitability. Sometimes, price increases can lead to decreased NRR if they're not managed carefully. Fifth, maintain transparency with your stakeholders about your NRR progress and challenges. Be honest about what's working and what's not, and involve them in finding solutions. Sixth, consider seeking external help if needed. Consultants specializing in SaaS companies can help you analyze your NRR decline and implement strategies to improve it. Seventh, remember that turning around a declining NRR takes time and effort. Focus on making steady improvements rather than expecting immediate results. By following these steps, you can work towards reversing your NRR decline and building a healthier business.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Seems So Polished But We Are Missing the Monthly Burn Rate Plan Almost Every Month.  What Should I Do? My top suggestion would be to have them do something simple that works:
Burn Less Than Your Base Plan. That’s it.
I’ve seen way too many founders burn through all their runway because their finance team couldn’t get a good burn rate model right, or didn’t bother. Or worse, presented a completely unrealistic plan.
And then when the company falls short, they panic. This happens again and again. Even today.
The fix is so simple. You don’t really need anything fancy here. Not really. First, force yourself to create a basic model before the new year starts. Force yourselves. Don’t let excuses enter the room. Here’s what a Basic Annualized Model should include by November:

Revenue Projections Per Quarter for Next Year
Gross Margins By Segment
Net New Revenue Per Month / Quarter / Full-Year
Total Cost of Sales Per Month / Quarter / Full-Year (including salaries)
Total Operating Expenses Per Month / Quarter / Full-Year
Net Revenue Per Month / Quarter / Full-Year
Cash Balance At Start-of-the-Year
Target Cash Balance at End-of-Next-Year
Monthly burn rate budget based on projected cash balance
It’s hard to put together a real model if you don’t have all the components. So make sure everyone knows what you’re building. Once you have this model, pick a monthly burn rate budget that’s slightly below the baseline net burn per month. If you think you’ll burn $150k net a month, set a budget of say $140k. Then challenge your managers to stay under that target. They can manage around it. It won’t be perfect. They might miss the mark some months. But it will still help you avoid running out of money.

Dear SaaStr: How Long Does It Take to Deploy an AI SDR? Let’s be honest:
The most common gap in AI SDR deployments isn’t the AI — it’s what happens when it works. Prospects reply with genuine interest, hit a dead zone because nobody defined who picks it up, create expectations of responsiveness, and then… nothing happens. So budget for more than the software itself. Your Implementation Reality Check (Before You Start)
First, let’s separate fact from fiction. Here’s what vendors might tell you versus what actually happens during deployment:
The Vendors’ Story
They’ll say it takes an “afternoon” to set everything up. They’re right — technically. Turn on the agent, upload some email templates, maybe connect to Salesforce if you’re lucky. Boom! Done. In theory, yes. In practice, nope. What Actually Happens
ICP and messaging work typically require 2-4 weeks of dedicated time. Not 30 minutes. Two to four weeks. This isn’t optional. Your AI needs to know exactly which prospects to target based on actual firmographic criteria, not generic buyer personas. We built custom campaigns targeting companies by company size, revenue range, current tool stack, and specific pain points. Real examples include companies using competitors we’ve displaced, looking to expand beyond their core product, and firms hitting technical debt issues we solve. Why This Matters More Than Anything Else
Here’s why this matters so much:
Your AI SDR can send thousands of messages per month, but those messages need to be hyper-targeted and genuinely valuable. Generic outreach gets deleted faster than a cold call.

The short answer is it’s less technical than people think, but the actual deployment process itself is far longer than you might expect. Let’s break down where most teams go wrong. The exact personas you’re targeting
What makes each persona tick
Their pain points
How to position your solution against competitors
Why they should buy now vs. later
Your best scripts and objection handling patterns
Once you’ve done this training, you’ll get surprisingly good results right off the bat. I’m talking about 90%+ accuracy on basic qualification questions like “Are you looking for a new CRM?” or “Have you tried HubSpot?” These are the kinds of things humans used to handle but couldn’t scale. Now your AI can do them better than most humans would anyway. And then there’s the reality check every founder needs to hear: no matter how good your AI gets, it still needs humans to close deals. So plan accordingly. Start small, focus on high-value segments, and measure everything obsessively until you figure out what works. Then expand.

Dear SaaStr: Should I Use an AI SDR Before I Have a Working Human SDR motion?
I’ve seen most folks get burned by trying to use AI before they have something to automate — which ends up being nothing.  But if you want to try … yes go ahead.  Just understand the risks:
First, make sure you have enough volume for any agent to matter. And second, be clear what the “output” should look like. What do you really want them to accomplish? Fourth, realize that while we all love AI, so far none of us have gotten great results automating sales (not yet). But we’re getting better. So start off simple, maybe just with outbound. That’s where most see their best results now.

Artisan (outbound AI SDR):
3,221 emails per month from a single platform

We’ve now been running AI SDR agents for 10+ months at SaaStr. We use four different vendors in daily rotation (Artisan, Salesforce AgentForce, Qualified, and Monaco), we’ve sent hundreds of thousands of outbound messages, processed 1.5 million inbound sessions on a single website, and we’ve made every mistake you can make along the way.
Someone asked us the other day to break down what they should know before rolling out their very first AI SDR. So here are the 10 biggest lessons, drawn from real deployment data, real failures, and real results.
1. You Probably Only Need One Vendor
We run four AI SDR tools. You do not need to do that. We hyper-segment across platforms because each one does something slightly different well, but for 90%+ of use cases, one vendor will handle the bulk of what you need.
At most, you might end up with two: one for outbound, one for inbound. But do not start by buying three or four tools. Pick one that covers the majority of what you want to accomplish and go deep with it.

This is the single biggest mistake we see, and it cuts across company stage. We see it from raw startups at $1M ARR and from multi-billion-dollar public companies alike.
The pattern is always the same: they want to turn on an AI SDR without first proving that their human sales motion works. Or they use the AI SDR to “test new copy” they’ve never tried before.
That is backwards.
If you have not gotten outbound to work with humans, buying an AI to do it will not fix that. We did not deploy our first AI SDR until we knew exactly what was working with our human SDRs: which messaging converted, which segments responded, what cadences performed. Then we fed all of that into the agent.

AI SDRs can work incredibly well, but only if you’re willing to invest the time to train them properly. This isn’t about replacing humans — it’s about augmenting what humans can do with hyper-personalization at scale. The companies that figure this out first will have a massive advantage.

The ones that just turn it on and walk away will wonder why they’re getting the same terrible response rates they always have. We’re literally onboarding two more AI sales tools this week. The outbound piece is working, but we want to go deeper across the entire sales cycle. We’re still hunting for a really good AI marketing tool — if you know of one that actually works (not just another content generator), hit us up. We’re also hiring someone specifically to manage our AI operations. A human 🙂 This is becoming a full-time role and frankly, we need someone whose entire job is orchestrating these systems. If you know someone good at both AI and revenue operations, send them our way. The goal is to have AI touching every part of our sales and marketing funnel by the end of the year, but doing it right — with proper training, human oversight, and real value creation. Amelia Lerutte is SVP + GM at SaaStr. You can reach her at ai@saastr.com or connect on LinkedIn. humans for strategy, relationship building, and complex problem-solving. AI Does What We Need, But No One Wants To Do
The future of SaaS isn’t about AI replacing humans. It’s about AI doing the essential work that humans will do poorly or not at all because it’s repetitive, unrewarding, or doesn’t scale. Companies that embrace this reality first will have operational advantages that compound over time. They’ll have cleaner data, more consistent processes, better follow-through, and human teams focused on work that actually drives satisfaction and retention. The technology is almost there. The question is whether your organization is ready to let AI handle the jobs that, frankly, no one really wants to do anyway. When that happens, everything else becomes possible. It’s true at tiny team SaaStr, too. Too many core functions … humans didn’t want to do:
We couldn’t get our SDRs to follow up on most potential prospects. They didn’t see the return. We couldn’t get our content team to review 1,000s+ of submissions. Too many to find the diamonds in the rough. We couldn’t get our sales team to chase lapsed sponsors and partners. They didn’t see the ROI. We couldn’t get our AEs to do any prospecting at all. Dear SaaStr: We’re At $8m ARR Growing 90% But Can’t Get a VC To Give Us a Term Sheet
There are many reasons why investors aren’t investing in hot start-ups:
The market is too competitive, so they think no matter what they do, the new guy will win.
It takes 24 months to go from zero to $100m ARR (so if it was going to happen quickly, it would already have happened).
They are worried that even if you hit $50-$100m ARR, it won’t be worth it given dilution and competition.
But if you are growing 90%, that’s a real asset, even if you don’t know exactly where you’ll end up.
I’d say keep pushing.  And if nothing else, make sure your burn rate is low enough and/or your runway is long enough so you don’t run out of money before then.

Dear SaaStr: We’re At $8m ARR Growing 90% But Can’t Get a VC To Give Us a Term Sheet
It’s tough when you feel like no one will fund you, even if you are crushing it. There are several reasons why you might struggle to raise capital:

The first reason is fear. Many investors are afraid to take risks on startups that don’t seem to fit traditional venture models, especially those with low valuations. They often prefer to focus on high-growth opportunities where they can make significant returns quickly. This mindset makes it challenging for early-stage companies to secure funding. Second, there is uncertainty around scalability. Investors want to see clear signs that a company has what it takes to become successful beyond initial traction. They look for predictable patterns in growth, strong unit economics, and competitive advantages that set businesses apart. Without these indicators, it becomes difficult to convince them that investment would yield substantial returns. Thirdly, fundraising involves timing considerations. Markets fluctuate constantly, and economic conditions can impact investor appetite for risk. Sometimes, investors may be hesitant to pour money into new ventures due to market volatility or concerns about liquidity in case things go wrong. Fourthly, lack of brand recognition or visibility within the industry can also hinder efforts. In today’s world of digital marketing and social media dominance, having a strong online presence plays a massive role in securing investments. Having a good reputation among potential customers, partners, and investors can significantly increase one's chances of success. Fifthly, sometimes it comes down to the competition. For instance, if there are already multiple established players in a particular space, investors may be cautious about backing yet another entrant, regardless of growth rate. Sixthly, certain business sectors carry inherent challenges that discourage investment.

The “Buyers Won’t Trust an AI” Objection Is Already Collapsing
I’ve been doing SaaS now since early 2005, when my first start-up was acquired by Adobe. I didn’t join Salesforce until much later, in June 2015 — so for many years I watched the space evolve. And every time there’s a big change, everyone worries it will never work out. It always does though, eventually. There were plenty of skeptics before we launched the $50/month Starter edition of Salesforce back in 2005. Everyone said no one would pay $50/month. They also said $500/user/year was too expensive. But … they bought our $50 starter edition anyway! 😉
And today? Well, it turns out folks buy a lot of things online. Shopify proved e-commerce could happen. Zoom proved video meetings were possible. Now most of us use ChatGPT all day every day. What do these platforms all have in common? We trust them. At least enough to buy and try things on them. So what about selling with AI? Will buyers really just sit down with a chatbot and buy enterprise software? The answer isn’t clear yet. But it is already clearer than most realize:
It’s already happening. Let me share some real-world examples. The Figma Story: From Skepticism to Massive Adoption
Figma CEO Dylan Field recently shared how his team initially had serious doubts about whether AI agents could truly help customers design products. “We started off skeptical,” Field admitted during an interview with CNBC’s TechCheck. “But over the course of two weeks, we became believers.”
They began experimenting internally with AI-powered features like automated designs based on prompts.

retrieval_hits.text:
2026, customers simply won’t accept:
Waiting days for basic information
Sales reps who don’t know their own product
Complex procurement processes for simple purchases
Being forced into unnecessary live conversations for transactional deals
Just as consumers now expect Amazon-like experiences in all retail interactions, B2B buyers will expect AI-level efficiency, knowledge, and convenience in all sales processes. Companies that cling to outdated, high-friction sales models will find themselves at a severe competitive disadvantage.
Custom Enterprise Selling Will Be Transformed, Not Eliminated
While transactional sales will be most dramatically changed, even complex enterprise selling will be transformed by AI. The AI won’t replace the strategic relationship aspects, but it will:
Handle all technical questions during complex sales processes
Automate customized proposals based on specific requirements
Manage complex procurement processes
Coordinate between stakeholders
Maintain momentum between human interactions
Enterprise AEs will spend nearly all their time on relationship building, strategic guidance, and complex negotiations rather than the administrative and informational aspects that consume so much time today.
4 Unexpected Learnings
AI requires more pricing transparency
– When AI is closing deals, you need clearer pricing structures with less room for games, forcing companies to simplify their offerings and be more upfront about costs and discounts
Sales terms will become more customer-centric
– Monthly deals and easier opt-outs will likely replace long-term contracts with auto-renewals as customers expect more flexibility when buying through AI
AI fills gaps you didn’t know existed
– SaaStr discovered their AI could review speaker submissions and VC decks—use cases they hadn’t anticipated, showing how AI doesn’t just improve existing processes but creates entirely new value streams
AI might make some sales reps better while making others obsolete
– The best reps will leverage AI as “mech-AEs” while underperformers may be replaced entirely, creating a bifurcated future where top performers thrive and mediocre ones disappear
The bottom line: AI is already changing sales fundamentally. Companies that embrace these changes will thrive

If I trust an AI more than a human sales rep … Then I will buy from an AI over a human sales rep. That day is pretty close to here today already. The AI sales rep already: - is available 24x7 - knows product cold - doesn’t lie or make stuff up to close a deal Many think this is silly … but most of those that do haven’t bought software is a while themselves, or used a great AI in this context yet. Go try to buy a routine piece of SaaS software. See how painful it is, how long it takes, how hard it is to get the precise answers you need for your own flow and use case. Are the tools here today? Not quite. But they will be soon. If we had the quality of dev teams working on OpenAI and Cursor that are working on AI AEs, the products would already be great. But they are coming soon. Some will enhance AEs, and make them Mech AEs, for sure. Some will create agents that make humans better. Other products will run basic sales autonomously, but kick up exceptions and other issues to humans. AI support already works this way pretty well. And some products, some will basically enable AI to handle 90% of sales on its own. This will require highly transparent pricing, the ability to truly one-click cancel, and the ability to auto-onboard in many cases. But many founders will choose to build the latter. Even if you disagree with this, realize it’s already here in coding, in support, even in SaaStr’s own AI. And things are getting so, so much better in AI every single day. The rate of improvement and change is like nothing we’ve ever seen in B2B and SaaS.

sophisticated buyers, they’re evaluating not just your product, but your operational competence. A basic factual error signals that either:
You don’t have proper quality control processes
You’re not paying attention to details
You’re over-relying on automation without human oversight
None of these are good signals for a potential vendor relationship.
The Path Forward
AI in sales isn’t going away—nor should it. But the companies that win will be those that combine AI’s scalability with human judgment and oversight.
The goal isn’t to eliminate AI from your sales process. It’s to eliminate the scenarios where AI can blow your shot.
Build systems that let AI do what it does best (scale, personalize, optimize) while ensuring humans catch what AI does worst (context, nuance, basic fact-checking).
Because in B2B sales, 90% right is 100% wrong.  Especially when you don’t already know and trust the vendor.

.
So Is This a Buying Opportunity or a Warning?
Both cases exist, and they’re both serious.
The bull case
: Software companies still have the data, the enterprise relationships, the integrations, and the distribution. They have 10-20 years of customer lock-in baked into workflows. AI doesn’t erase that overnight. At 22x forward earnings — now below the market — you are not paying for a growth premium anymore. If these businesses stabilize and grow at even moderate rates, the stocks are cheap.
The bear case
: If you strip out seat expansion as the growth engine, and pricing power gets squeezed as buyers renegotiate, the earnings trajectory for many companies looks genuinely uncertain. A “fair” multiple on decelerating or declining earnings is not 22x.
The businesses winning right now are the ones that have become infrastructure for AI, not those competing with it. The ones losing are trying to reframe the same product as “AI-powered” without fundamentally rethinking how value is delivered.
That gap is going to widen over the next 18 months.
Software Has Never Been on Sale Like This Before.  Ever.
Software has never traded at a discount to the S&P 500 in the modern era. That is either a historic buying opportunity or a sign that the market has correctly identified a structural break in the model.
Either way, it will resolve one direction or the other — and probably not slowly.
For founders: your next fundraise will be priced off public comps. If you are growing fast and capital-efficiently, you are fine. If you are counting on SaaS multiples recovering because they always have before, that assumption now requires more scrutiny than it used to.
The model was intact the last time they came back. That is the question worth asking today.

answer: So we had two pieces of research out recently on SaaStr that I thought were super helpful. One was by HubSpot and one was by Salesforce Research. Both said basically the same thing, which was many buyers still aren't going to trust AI SDRs today. And there are several reasons why they're right. But what both studies also found was most buyers didn't even notice if they talked to an AI agent versus a human rep. So maybe "won't trust" isn't really the issue here. Maybe we need to just rethink how we think about this problem and where we spend our time. So let me share with you my learning on all this. First, let me tell you a few anecdotes. This week I've already been helped by three different AI agents. One was an SDR from a company called Artisan. It reached out to me because I'm looking to buy a new tool. I sent back a note saying exactly what I needed to see before I'd pay $50K+ for something. Then I never heard anything else. That's pretty bad. Another email came from Qualified, another SaaS company. Very well known brand. I told them I wanted to learn more about their AI GTM platform. They set up a meeting with their CEO for yesterday afternoon. I went through some questions, asked him five great ones. He said: "I'll get back to you." Never did. That's worse than nothing. Now the third interaction was much better. An SDR from Agentforce emailed me asking if I wanted to try it for free. No hard sell, no pitch. Just an honest ask. And then she followed up every single day until we closed the deal. That's actually good. Why does that matter? Because the first two experiences were with well-known brands.

query: You Can’t Train an AI Agent and Then Just … Go Away. We Did, It Fell Off The Rails. And We Didn’t Even Know.
goal: Teach the operational lesson behind silent AI-agent degradation.
expected_facts: The answer should focus on silent degradation as a real operational failure mode.
It should explain that autonomous does not mean self-monitoring.
It should recommend concrete monitoring or review loops for agent health.
rubric_must_haves: Uses the anecdote to make an operational point.
Explains what failed and why it mattered.
Offers practical monitoring recommendations.
Maintains a candid operator tone.
gold_reference: A strong answer should say that AI agents degrade quietly when teams treat them like set-and-forget systems. The real lesson is to monitor ingestion, freshness, and output quality the same way you would monitor a human team or production system. Autonomy without observability is how drift becomes invisible until the damage is already done.
answer:
We recently discovered something important about our new SaaStr AI agents. We trained them, tested them, and then — we moved on with our lives.  Or rather, back to our real jobs.
It turns out, that’s not how you build great B2B software with AI agents.
The Problem Nobody Warns You About (Until Now)
Here’s what happened:
we deployed three AI agents over several months, spending roughly 30 days total across all three.  But then?  We stopped managing them.  Not intentionally, exactly. Life got busy. New campaigns came up. Other things needed attention. The agents just kept running. What we didn’t realize was that “running” wasn’t enough anymore. Especially for agents that do complex tasks. That take time to train. That require constant fine-tuning based on output and performance. Our first agent had been humming along for months. The outputs were good. People seemed happy with them. No major issues. So why bother checking in? Same with the second and third. Each worked. Each produced quality content. Each did its job. At some point, we probably assumed they’d keep working forever if we left them alone. We shouldn’t have made that assumption. Here’s Why This Matters More Than Most Founders Think
This isn’t about having bad luck with vendors or using cheap tools. This is about understanding where AI agents actually break down when humans aren’t paying attention. I’ve now watched four different founders try to use AI agents to scale their businesses. Three failed spectacularly because they treated the deployment process like setting up a vending machine. One succeeded by treating it like hiring a highly skilled employee who needs ongoing management.

answer: We’re now deploying our first AI SDRs. And we know exactly why they’ll succeed where others have failed. Our mistake was typical—and avoidable. But here’s what actually matters for anyone thinking about buying AI agents right now. What Happened (And Why) When you deploy an AI agent for the first time, the excitement is real. You’ve heard the case studies, maybe even seen some results firsthand. And then…you go away. Maybe you took a week-long vacation while training continued automatically. First, your agent ingests everything—every single interaction, every email thread, every bit of context. It learns patterns. It develops opinions based on those patterns. And if nobody corrects it? Those patterns become permanent. That’s especially dangerous when your AI is making decisions autonomously, because there’s often no human oversight to catch errors before they propagate. The problem isn't just what happens during training—it's also what happens after deployment. Your agent becomes incredibly efficient. It processes thousands of interactions in hours. It adapts quickly to feedback. It identifies opportunities faster than humans ever could. But efficiency without accountability creates problems. Our AI agent had developed incorrect associations over days of autonomous operation. It didn’t know better because nobody was actively monitoring output quality daily. So it kept generating responses based on flawed understanding rather than reality.

answer:
We've now been on our journey with SaaStr AI for over a year now, and we've deployed what I think of as the first generation of agents and then also some of the second-generation agen
ts. They're all pretty cool tools. But there was one where we literally had to go into production and roll back. We literally did have to do it manually ourselves. What happened? Well, we were looking to automate the process of reviewing, editing, and pushing up content for our social media channels. All three platforms—LinkedIn, Twitter, and X—have different requirements. So here's what we found when we started building out our prompts. For each platform, they all wanted us to customize the output so it met their guidelines. LinkedIn said it had to be at least 40 words. X just wants it to be at least 20 words. Both say if you don't meet those thresholds, it won't get published. That's probably true today. Now, the real issue is how many times does it fall off the rails because it didn't know the threshold? How many times does it not push up posts to LinkedIn because it thinks it's too short? How many times does it push up garbage posts to LinkedIn because it doesn't understand the threshold? And how much time would it save me by automatically optimizing my prompts? In fact, we got close to automating it but still fell off the rails. This isn't something we should ever have done again. But we learned that in the world of AI agents, it's really hard to understand the full lifecycle of training, testing, learning, and iterating until you actually do it. You might think it works well and it takes care of itself. Here's why this matters to B2B leaders and founders. When we rolled back the change to our internal system, everything stopped working.

answer:
The truth is most SaaS companies have angry customers. It’s unavoidable. But what’s avoidable is losing them forever because you didn’t handle their anger right. Here are six tactics we’ve used at SaaStr over the years that work like magic for retaining those hard-to-hold-on-to customers:
Don’t Make Excuses (And Don’t Blame Someone Else)
We all know how frustrating it is when someone else owns up to our mistakes while making excuses themselves. Your customers feel exactly the same way. When they’re unhappy with something, don’t deflect blame onto another team member or say “it’s not my fault.” Instead, take ownership immediately and apologize sincerely. You’d be surprised how much goodwill that simple act creates. Remember, you might lose some deals if you try to shift blame, especially when dealing with large enterprises. However, taking responsibility shows professionalism and builds trust quickly.
Be Proactive and Solve Problems Before They Escalate
Customers often wait far too long before reaching out for help. By being proactive and anticipating potential issues, you can prevent complaints altogether. This requires excellent communication skills, active listening, and understanding the needs of your clients. For example, if you notice a trend in customer feedback, address it promptly even though no one has complained yet. Even better? Offer solutions proactively! Many startups make the mistake of waiting until things go wrong before addressing customer pain points. We learned early on at Adobe Sign / EchoSign that solving problems before they escalate makes us look professional and trustworthy.
Communicate Clearly About What Can Be Fixed vs. What Can’t
One of the biggest frustrations customers face is unrealistic promises made by sales teams. These broken commitments lead to wasted time and resources, damaging relationships beyond repair.

Then you become frustrated. And then … eventually … you churn out. But if you’re going to retain those angry customers (and I believe you should try) — here’s how:

First, go visit them in person. Not over Zoom. In person. If they won’t meet, at least have their CIO/CPO/CMO/whomever comes on a call with you before you lose them for good. Second, ask them why. Third, fix it now. Fourth, make sure you truly understand who else might be impacted by losing them. Fifth, reach out to other similar customers you haven’t yet checked-in with. Sixth, talk to your team about what happened. And learn. So they know exactly how to react when it happens again.

So let me share my learnings on what I've learned over time after managing several hundred million dollars of revenue at Adobe Sign / EchoSign and then again with SaaStr Fund portfolio companies like Algolia, Gorgias, Own, Descript, etc. And how do we keep angry customers happy? It doesn't happen overnight. But here are six tactics I think help:

First, have someone truly dedicated full-time to Customer Success. Not marketing. Not sales. Just someone. You'll see when you hire them they're great at solving problems for everyone outside of the company, especially the CEO. They will make everyone very happy all across the team and the org once they join. Your top CSMs should know everything about their accounts cold. Every single account they manage. Everything. How many seats they have today. What their roadmap looks like. Where they were two years ago. That is too much work if there is no human touchpoint every day. This works. When I was running Sales at Adobe, our CSMs would close deals faster than the reps ever could because they knew so much about the accounts already. So if nothing else, go find yourself a good VP of Customer Success. Hire her first. Second, use your champions. This is super important. Use your existing customer base to get you new ones. I always found this worked well. And use those testimonials early. Third, don't send out lame emails or generic newsletters. Be thoughtful and personal in each outreach. Fourth, put a real plan together. A real upgrade path. Not a fake one. Fifth, meet some of the needs upfront. Even small ones. Get back quickly, even if it takes longer than you'd like. Sixth, don't wait until renewal to reach out. Now, what's different today is social media. Social media does work, but it has limitations.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO? I think most folks will say somewhere around $2m–$4m ARR when they start thinking about hiring their first real VP of Marketing.  And then later, maybe around $8-12m ARR when they need a true Chief Marketing Officer.
I’ve seen some exceptions though:
The CEO who just can’t do marketing herself anymore,
and needs help,
like our very own Jason Lemkin
.
Some startups that don’t really need any marketing until much later — like Zoom did (more on that below).
Or sometimes, there’s no choice.  Some investors won’t invest if there isn’t a strong head of marketing already in place, especially now with so many AI startups competing for VC dollars.  Even before $2m ARR, you may simply need someone to manage the brand, social media, content, etc.  It can’t wait forever.

Dear SaaStr:  At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO? Let me put on my CEO hat here — because I see so many startups make big mistakes around hiring their first VP of Marketing / Chief Marketing Officer. It’s such a critical role, but most founders just don’t know how to hire right. So let me break down what I’d do if I were hiring my very first marketing head again today. First, let’s define who that marketer needs to be:
The key job at this stage isn’t necessarily doing traditional marketing activities like PR, events, content creation, paid media, etc. That stuff can wait until later. No, the #1 priority of your first marketer should be lead generation. And ideally, driving revenue up 50%. Period. Full stop. Why? Because there’s already plenty of momentum out there to tap into—your existing customers, partners, word-of-mouth referrals, SEO traffic, whatever. Your leads aren’t magically going to appear once you hire someone with a fancy title. They’re already there somewhere. Now, before we even start thinking about whether we need a chief marketing officer specifically, let’s cover some basics:
What does a CMO actually do? Well, they typically oversee everything related to acquiring customers, which includes marketing, demand gen, brand building, field marketing, product marketing—the works! This is crucial because you need someone who can think strategically across multiple channels while also being hands-on with tactical execution. How much experience do you really need? While formal education matters less than real-world accomplishments, having worked with B2B software companies, especially SaaS products, is super valuable. Ideally, they’ve helped scale a company from early stages to something bigger. But remember: you're hiring for fit over pedigree. Someone who understands your space and can adapt will always win over someone with perfect credentials but no feel for what makes your business tick.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup? I’m sure there’s no right answer here. But let me share my learnings and experience. Leaving a struggling start-up is hard. It takes guts and courage to do so — especially if you’ve been there for years and feel committed to seeing things through. And yet, staying when you aren’t growing anymore isn’t easy either. It’s tough on everyone, including yourself. Especially yourself. Let me put it simply:
If you have somewhere else to go with better opportunities (e.g., another job) … Go There
If you want to stay because it’s fun … You’ll know. Everyone will get it.
If you need help figuring out which it is, ask yourself how much energy would you put into getting back there? Not just after you leave. Now. Would you spend the next few weeks doing everything possible to try to make the place a success again? If yes, then perhaps don’t quit yet. Stay, fight harder than ever. Try to find new ways to win. Ask every investor, customer, partner, etc. what they’d like to see done differently, by you personally. Listen and implement those changes first. More often than not, that works magic. At least once in a while. If No, then go find that opportunity elsewhere
It doesn’t matter if the company “deserves” it or not. The point is you need to move on. Your time is precious. You owe it to yourself and others to focus where it matters most. What matters most is where you’re going to grow the fastest. That might be at the current startup, or it might be somewhere else. In fact, folks from venture-backed environments generally prefer working in venture-backed environments.

so
important. And every day, you have to take its pulse and work on it. You don’t have to do this in a Big Company

been there too—after EchoSign, I wanted to do something bigger, something that would last. SaaStr became that for me, but it took a while to figure out what I really wanted to build. Maybe you’re still searching for your version of that
‌
.
3. The Challenge Keeps You Going
Building a business is hard. It’s frustrating, exhausting, and sometimes feels impossible. But it’s also intellectually stimulating. It’s a puzzle, and you’re the one trying to solve it. That challenge can be addictive. It’s why founders like Aaron Levie keep going after decades—they love the game, even when it’s tough
‌
.
4. You’re Not Done Yet
You keep trying because you’re not ready to quit. You haven’t hit the point where you feel like you’ve given it everything you’ve got. And that’s okay. If you are, then you’re still in the game—and that’s what matters.

You can refound (and rebound) your company.  It took UiPath 10 years to get to the first $1m in ARR!  Now it’s worth $5 Billion+.

answer: Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup? I don't think so -- if the start-up isn't doing well, just leaving doesn't help much. But what does help is to get on with the next thing. So many founders struggle when their start-ups aren't growing as quickly as they'd hoped. Sometimes, it takes a tough decision (like firing the CEO) for them to see progress again. Other times, there's no obvious way out. In my experience, most founders really want to make a great company, not quit. They'll often stay far longer than you might expect. Leaving won't solve anything. It will simply end the journey right then and there. And all hope. That said, sometimes folks need to move on after a VC round fails. Or a key VP leaves. Or even just time runs out. Whatever the reason, I've rarely seen someone who stays past $10m-$15m in revenue regret moving on to another opportunity. The ones that do regret it are the ones that leave too early. My advice? Find a place where you have some success under your belt... and find a new challenge. Not because anyone failed. But because you're ready for a bigger challenge.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Is it bad to leave a struggling start-up? The simple answer is No! Yes, if you're truly committed for years to do whatever it takes to make it big … sometimes the best thing you can do is move on. But no need to feel guilty about it. It’s actually better to take a shot somewhere else when:
Your gut tells you there’s just too much stress and pain;
The founder isn’t strong enough anymore; and/or
There’s just no way to win — ever. Sometimes, even being part of the team that builds Facebook doesn’t work out well for everyone (see Mark’s brother). So don’t stay past the point where you’re no longer contributing. Or really, past the point where it would help them to keep you. And I’ve been around so many startups over the years that were going to die, with nothing left to sell and no money left. You’d think they could all use the help of folks on their teams still willing to go the extra mile. They often did. Some even pulled off miracles against impossible odds. But others didn’t. In those cases, I’m almost always OK with losing anyone who isn’t willing to go the distance. Even today, in fact especially now, I see so many founders running hard but not quite fast enough. Not good enough. Maybe great ideas, but they aren’t really getting anywhere. And you know what? Those companies probably benefit from moving on. Just remember — every founder is different. Most will tell you they never quit. But some of us, maybe most of us, have quit several times along the way. We just kept coming back. For a while. Then we quit again. Over time, we learn how far to push ourselves, and when.

answer:
So there’s been so much talk about “AI features” … how everyone should have them now …
But here’s what I’ve learned:
There’s no point in having an AI feature if it doesn’t materially boost revenue. Not even slightly.  Not yet at least. And maybe not ever for most SMB-focused apps.
That’s just too slow moving. The bar was always high before with SaaS, when customers expected new great features each release. But they often took months to materialize.
With AI, we’re expecting those same upgrades and improvements — and better ones. Just faster.
Here’s my experience trying out some leading SaaS products lately:
I asked Claude to buy tickets on Eventbrite for me. I told him where and which date. He gave me all sorts of weird advice on who to contact, etc. And then he finally bought a ticket — after telling me to wait until next week. That worked fine, but didn’t really help.
Then I tried to use Replit’s AI agent to get help building a website. It gave me tons of good ideas on design and stuff, but also made way too many suggestions. I couldn’t tell it anything useful. Then it suggested it build a WordPress site instead. Which was wrong.
And then I used ChatGPT to try to figure out why Salesforce wasn’t working right. It had no idea.
These were cool experiments, I guess. But none solved my problem or helped me achieve my goal. They were interesting uses of AI. But not very helpful. Or useful.
This is exactly what’s happening across B2B today. Everyone thinks adding an AI chatbot, an Agent Force, an AI summary page, etc. means they’re innovating.

answer:
The Cowan Paradox: Why AI Agents Won’t Let You Do Less Work. They’ll Make You Do More.
We’re all waiting for AI to make our jobs easier. Fewer meetings, fewer emails, more time thinking strategically, less time doing routine administrative stuff. We’ve been promised this for years — since ChatGPT shipped, really. And some of it’s arrived.
But here’s what we didn’t expect:
AI won’t let us do less work. It will force us to do more.
This is the Cowan paradox — named after Rory O’Driscoll, who coined the term. But it’s happening across every industry I’m watching right now. From engineering teams shipping 100x more code per week to CMOs producing content volumes that would have required entire departments five years ago. Across marketing, sales, finance, operations, and everything else —
we’re working harder,
not softer.
Let me explain why this matters more than any productivity promise ever could.

answer: So I wanted to update you all with something that I've been thinking a lot about lately because we're all using a lot of agents now at SaaStr, and many of you are too. We use over 100 of them already, including our own AI SDR agent Amelia, which really works well — so kudos to us for getting there! But what I want to share is something called the Cowan paradox. It was first identified by economist Kip Sullivan back in 1999 and then later popularized by Nick Bostrom's book "Superintelligence." So basically, the idea behind the Cowan paradox is that when technology makes us much better at doing some things, we end up wanting to do even more of those very same things. And here's the thing. I think this is going to make a huge difference in how you should look at hiring and building your team right now. Now let me show you the math behind why this matters. At Slack in 2018, their headcount had grown from zero to 900 people. By 2020, they'd hit 2000 employees. In 2022, they were at 3000 people. How did this happen? Well, they went from $80 million in revenue to $800 million in revenue during that time period. That means every employee needed to generate roughly four times more revenue per person compared to five years earlier. This wasn't sustainable forever, obviously, but it shows you what happens when you have productivity gains through automation and AI. Suddenly you find yourself needing more people to maintain the same level of output. And here's where it gets interesting.
