answer:
The AI Age Is Here—But Not Everyone’s Ready
We’re living through what feels like the most significant technological shift since mobile devices changed how we consume information. For B2B software companies specifically, I believe the next three years will bring more disruption than the previous decade combined. And it starts with something incredibly counterintuitive:
the rise of the “N=1 app.”
What Are We Actually Talking About? This isn’t just another buzzword. In fact, many founders have already built their first N-1 apps—and they’ve been surprised by how addictive (and useful) they are. So let me break down exactly what we mean here. What Is An N=1 Application? An N=1 application is essentially a highly specialized tool you build yourself using no-code platforms like Replit or Lovable. Think of it as a personal assistant that helps you automate repetitive tasks across multiple tools and services. Unlike generic workflows that connect dozens of third-party integrations, an N=1 app solves a single problem for you perfectly. Why This Matters More Than You Realize
Let’s talk about why this matters beyond the hype cycle. First, the pace of change in AI-powered SaaS has accelerated dramatically over the past year. New capabilities emerge almost daily, making traditional enterprise software feel like it was built for a different era. Second, buying off-the-shelf solutions often means settling for functionality that doesn’t fully meet your needs. Generic workflows try to solve every use case simultaneously, resulting in interfaces cluttered with features you’ll never actually use. Third, if you’re running a business today, you don’t need to convince anyone else that AI is real—it’s already transforming every aspect of operations, from support tickets to pipeline management.

goal: Explain when custom internal AI software is the right choice.

answer:
The Rise of the “N=1” App: When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It
Let me tell you what’s happening right now across thousands of B2B companies, and why I think we’re entering a completely new era of software buying—especially among founders. We’ve all been there:
you need something done, maybe it doesn’t exist yet, so you just build it yourself. And then you look around and see everyone else doing the same thing. In fact, you’ll probably hear someone say, “Hey, they built their own CRM.” Or “They made their own dashboard.”
But here’s the problem with those stories: they don’t work most of the time because they were built before AI agents could do it better. There was no way to get things done that weren’t super manual and required too much human intervention. That’s changing fast. I’m seeing companies go from zero to hero on agent deployment over the course of months. They start with basic automation tools like Zapier and HubSpot workflows, move into proper agent platforms like Qualified and Artisan, and end up building complex internal systems that run autonomously while humans focus on high-value activities rather than low-leverage tasks. This isn’t about replacing people—it’s about amplifying them. Think about it: if you have a great SDR who wants to close six-figure deals versus a mediocre one trying to book meetings, which one deserves the best tools? The answer used to be obvious—you gave the closer the fancy CRM and the warmer leads. Now I’d argue you should give them whatever tool makes them even faster and better. Because when your top performers scale, your entire company scales. Why Custom Is Back (And Why Your Competitors Are Panicked)
Here’s what’s really interesting—and what every founder needs to understand: there’s a growing movement toward custom-built applications within companies. Not necessarily bespoke development, but often using off-the-shelf products with significant configuration and customization.

So I’m seeing two very different playbooks for sales hiring at hot AI B2B start-ups:
The “Traditional” Approach (Most Of Us Are Still Using)
Hire 200+ reps ASAP with lots of quota attainment requirements so everyone is incentivized to hit their number
At least 30% of new hires fail because they want too much time upfront to learn the product
High churn rate across all roles
Rely heavily on “SDRs” sending generic emails to warm prospects
Customer success team acts mainly as problem-solver when customers have issues
Solutions engineers spend most of their time building demos and training customers before the deal closes
Customer support team provides generic answers while waiting for solutions engineer input
The AI-Fueled Revolution Approach (Less Common But Interesting):
Focus on high-quality over quantity – hire fewer, better-performing reps
More emphasis on self-learning through hands-on experience rather than lengthy training periods
Higher expectations for productivity and results, but also higher rewards for achievement
Emphasis on speed-to-value delivery over extensive hand-holding throughout implementation
Direct customer communication becomes more efficient due to rapid response capabilities
AI tools enhance research and initial outreach efficiency
This approach seems to work best when there’s genuine market pull—customers actively seeking out the solution—and when the technology genuinely solves a previously unsolved problem. When those conditions aren’t met, the “traditional” playbook might actually perform worse due to its inherent inefficiencies.

answer:
So we've been talking for years with some of our top speakers like Sam Blond, now running Apollo.io, his old boss Kyle Norton who runs Outreach, and others, how big of a sales team should I have?
And if you're going to grow really quickly, well, most people will tell you that you gotta hire a ton of reps and make sure they're all hitting quota. That's the way we learned back in the day, right? It was Salesforce, HubSpot, Zoom, Slack—when those guys were growing quickly, their sales teams were massive because they had to close hundreds, thousands of customers to keep growing that fast.
But then we saw something weird happen when the first wave of AI agents came out. They didn't disrupt everything overnight. But what did change is this dynamic where SaaS startup founders would say, "Wait a minute, if I'm selling to a small company, maybe I can get away with having no sales team."
That's not new. We used to call them self-service companies. There always were two playbooks. Some folks wanted 1000s of reps to scale. Others said, "No, let me sell myself. Let me use software to automate some things." And there are so many great examples today.
I recently invested in a company called Replit. Their founder Amjad Masad is super smart. He sold himself into $300 million deal to Microsoft. Today, Replit sells itself to millions of developers, which is awesome. But they also added salespeople later. So here are the two playbooks:
The first playbook is, "Hey, I'll go buy Agent Force, I'll deploy Fin, I'll train my agents, and I'll figure out how to get them working so I don't even need a sales team anymore."
This is what Harvey does.

answer:
How do I make sure my SaaS business doesn’t run out of cash?  It’s so easy to fall behind here …
My Top 5 Mistakes As A Founder (So Far) — And How They Almost Killed Me
I’ve seen far too many founders quietly slide into trouble with their burn rate. They might still appear successful on paper – strong revenue growth, happy customers, expanding product offerings. But beneath the surface, they’re drowning in red ink.
As someone who’s been there myself, I can tell you exactly how to avoid this trap. It all comes down to transparency and planning:
The Hidden Danger Lurking In Every Board Meeting
Let me start with something counterintuitive: most boards don’t know if you’ll actually hit your next round. The brutal truth is that while everyone talks about runway management during board meetings, actual discussions around zero-cash date calculations rarely happen. Founders often skip sharing real figures because they feel like talking about their true runway will lead investors to think less of them. But hiding this information creates more problems than it solves. When you finally do need funding, having had months-long discussions about needing capital makes everything much easier. You already know what your options are, which boards want to meet with you, and why investors should believe in your vision. This isn’t just theoretical advice—this is based on firsthand experience. During our last raise, we were able to get meetings set up before even sending over pitch decks because we’d previously discussed our needs openly.

answer:
So I want to just talk to founders on how to make sure they don't run out of cash. There are two things that really help, two that will always work if you do 'em well enough, if you do 'em consistently. But like most advice, there's also some nuance here. The first thing I'm going to tell you to do is create four to five crisp, clear business objectives for the year. Now, why would we even care? Why does that matter? It matters because almost everyone in your team is going to forget what their goal was by week three. Everyone knows what they need to do every day, but very few people know where they're actually going longer term than maybe six months. And so when folks hear "four to five key objectives," they say, "Oh yeah, I already got those. My boss told me." Well, let me challenge you with a little bit different way of thinking about it. When you go into a board meeting and someone asks you — and probably you'll get asked this in a VCs' board meeting later, too — "What are your top four objectives?" You should literally look up at him, smile and say, "Well, Bob, I've got my slides right over here. Let me show you."
And then you pull them up and you clearly present each of those four to five objectives. What did you achieve in the prior quarter? Where do you stand today? And where do you hope to end up? This forces you to think about it. Even if it doesn't force you to put it together, it forces you to think through all the important stuff. Now, I know some folks might say, "Hey, isn't this just like our OKR framework?"
It is similar.

answer: So our first issue here when we went all-in with agentic AI was not having enough people around us who understood how to use it. We're lucky because we got some really great help from Cursor, Replit, and other vendors. We got training from Lovable. But we didn't even understand what questions to ask. So for example, if you want to vibe code an app, which you probably should do in the early days—just try it out—you need to know how to tell the AI exactly what you want done. You cannot tell it vaguely like "I want a sales tool." You have to say exactly what you mean. And then it works beautifully. But we couldn't figure it out until someone trained us. That's number one. Number two, the cost of mistakes is much higher than pre-AI times. In fact, it almost always is. Our worst incident took five weeks to resolve. Five weeks! It wasn't the end of the world, but it was super frustrating. When you make a mistake using a human team, maybe someone leaves and it takes six months to find another good hire. But when you make a mistake with an AI agent, it's instant. There's no recovery time. It happens right away. The stakes feel lower because there's less emotional attachment, but they feel higher because everything goes wrong so fast. And then we also found ourselves accidentally pushing agents into harm's way, giving them too many responsibilities too quickly, expecting things they weren't capable of. That's the third thing. Fourth is something called the primary source grounded claim problem. Think of it like asking ChatGPT to summarize a podcast episode. ChatGPT is going to quote every single guest, even though only one of those guests actually said anything worth quoting. So when you ask an AI agent to generate content based on what others have said, it tends to create a soup of everyone else's quotes rather than creating original value.

answer:
So I've been doing SaaStr for almost 15 years now, since 2007.
And my job — my job, our job, is to help founders build better start-ups. To find ways to grow faster. And then when they're ready, to go public. All that stuff.
But here's what I think I can tell you with some confidence after all those years:
There have never been harder times to raise venture capital than today.
Not even close. Not ever. It was hard before Covid hit us. We were all trying to get back into office by late 2019, early 2020. But things weren't great, but they were good. There was a lot of money out there.
Then Covid hit, which wasn't fun. No one had really seen anything like it. But many folks adapted. Cloud exploded. Zoom exploded. Slack exploded. And actually, in terms of VC funding, it got pretty darn good again. Because everyone wanted to invest in the winners of Covid. So if you could win during Covid, boy, did VCs want to fund you.
And then we went through this big downturn in '22. Inflation, interest rates up, et cetera. Everyone said it would be over by mid-'23. Then AI came along and everything changed. But even though the market rebounded, there just hasn't been enough money to go around since then. Folks that aren't seeing strong growth are struggling to raise capital. Some that do see growth often struggle to raise as much as they'd hoped for their stage. It's tough. I wish I had some magic advice on how to solve it, because I don't know exactly how to do it myself.
But let me say one thing that I am sure about. What worked in SaaS before, especially in 2021, doesn't work anymore. And so maybe we should stop talking about it too much. Let me explain why.
